questions.question: Explain why north-facing slopes are the warm slopes in South African valleys, and state when and in which valley orientation the aspect contrast is greatest.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa lies in the Southern Hemisphere, so the midday sun stands in the northern sky. A north-facing slope leans toward the sun: rays strike it at a steep, near-perpendicular angle, concentrating energy per square metre, and the slope is lit for more hours each day. A south-facing slope receives the same rays at a glancing angle spread over a wider area, so it stays cooler, shadier and moister. The contrast is greatest in winter, when the low sun exaggerates the angle difference, and in east-west valleys, where one wall faces due north and the other due south.

questions.question: Describe how a clear winter night builds a valley temperature inversion, and name and locate the warm zone that results.
questions.expected_answer: After sunset the slopes lose heat rapidly by long-wave radiation; air in contact with them chills, becomes denser, and drains downslope under gravity as katabatic wind. Cold air from both walls ponds on the valley floor, so by the early hours the coldest air lies at the bottom with warmer air above — temperature increases with height, inverting the normal pattern. The warm zone is the thermal belt: the mid-slope band above the ponded cold air and below the radiatively cooled upper slopes, the warmest part of the night-time valley.

questions.question: Account for the location of frost-sensitive orchards, farmsteads and transport routes in a fruit-growing valley such as the Langkloof, and identify one planning failure with its correction.
questions.expected_answer: Frost-sensitive orchards and vineyards occupy the thermal belt on the mid-slope, above the valley-floor frost pockets and below the short-season heights, with sun-demanding crops on the warm north-facing wall; hardy crops such as pasture and lucerne take the risky floor with its deep alluvial soils. Farmsteads sit on the lower slopes on or near the thermal belt, above the flood line and the worst frost. Roads and railways follow the flat floor and accept the radiation-fog risk. The planning failure is placing low-cost housing on cheap valley-floor land — the coldest, foggiest, smokiest, most flood-prone zone; the correction is housing on the mid-slope shelf, industry out of the inversion pond, and the floor reserved for fields, parks and the floodplain.
